course.title: SQL transactions and application code
course.description: Atomic multi-statement writes with rollback, lost updates and the versioned UPDATE, bound parameters against injection, upsert, and keyset pagination written in SQL.

unit.title: A transfer that rolls back on failure

tests.name: moves the amount and keeps the total unchanged
insufficient funds: throws and both balances are unchanged
an unknown destination: throws and the source keeps its money (trap)
an unknown source: throws and the destination gains nothing
a zero, negative or fractional amount is refused (boundary)
no transaction is left open after a failure

unit.title: A versioned UPDATE that reports conflicts

tests.name: a matching version writes the title and returns the next version
a stale version returns a conflict with the stored version and writes nothing
an unknown id returns not_found
two editors with the same version: the first wins, the second gets a conflict
a writer who commits between your statements is not overwritten (trap)
the title is bound as a value: quotes and SQL in it are stored as typed (boundary)

unit.title: A search that an injection string cannot widen

tests.name: finds the tenant's products whose name contains the term, ignoring case
never returns another tenant's rows
an injection string in the term cannot widen the result (trap)
an injection string in the tenant id cannot widen the result
a quote in the term is an ordinary character
a percent sign or an underscore in the term matches only itself (boundary)

fund-js/24-sql-transactions-and-app-code.instructions:
**Skills:** transactions · rollback · changed-row count  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Move money between two accounts. Now tell me every way this can leave the data wrong."

**Why it matters.** Two updates are two chances to stop in the middle. And one of the failure modes throws no error at all: an update aimed at an account that does not exist changes nothing and reports success.

**The database.** `db` is a synchronous SQLite handle (Node's `node:sqlite`): `db.exec(sql)` runs statements, and `db.prepare(sql).run(...params)` returns an object whose `changes` property is the number of changed rows. The table is `accounts(id, balance)` with a check constraint that keeps `balance` at zero or above.

**Your task.** Export `transfer(db, fromId, toId, amount)`. On success it moves `amount` from one account to the other and returns nothing. It throws an `Error`, and leaves every balance exactly as it was, when:
- `amount` is not a positive integer
- either account does not exist
- the source account does not hold enough

After a failed call no transaction may be left open on `db`: the next call must work normally.

**Worked example.** Account 1 holds 100 and account 99 does not exist. A transfer of 40 from 1 to 99 throws, and account 1 still holds 100.
hints: Atomicity: a group of statements that either all take effect or all disappear.
Open one unit of work around both writes, undo it on every failure path before passing the error on, and treat a write that touched no row as a failure even though the database did not complain.

Validate the amount first, then begin a transaction, run the debit and the credit, throw when either reports a changed-row count other than one, commit at the end, and in the catch block roll back and rethrow.

fund-js/24-sql-transactions-and-app-code.instructions:
**Skills:** optimistic concurrency · conditional UPDATE · changed-row count  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Two people edit the same document. The second save silently overwrites the first. Fix it in the data layer."

**Why it matters.** Reading the version, comparing it in JavaScript and then writing is a check followed by an act: another request can commit between the two statements. The comparison has to happen inside the statement that writes.

**The database.** `db` is a synchronous SQLite handle (Node's `node:sqlite`): `db.prepare(sql).run(...params)` returns an object with a `changes` count, and `db.prepare(sql).get(...params)` returns one row or `undefined`. The table is `docs(id, title, version)`.

**Your task.** Export `updateTitle(db, id, title, expectedVersion)`. It returns:
- `{ status: 'ok', version }` with the new version (the old one plus one) when the stored version equals `expectedVersion`; the title is written
- `{ status: 'conflict', version }` with the version now stored when the row exists but its version differs; nothing is written
- `{ status: 'not_found' }` when no row has that id

Do not open a transaction. One test lets another writer commit between two of your statements, the way a second request would; that writer's title must survive.

**Worked example.** The document is at version 1. A save with `expectedVersion` 1 returns `{ status: 'ok', version: 2 }`. A second save that still says 1 returns `{ status: 'conflict', version: 2 }`.
hints: Optimistic concurrency: the write itself must verify that the row is still the one the client saw.

Make the expected version part of the condition that selects the row to change, then let the number of rows the write touched tell you whether it happened. Only look the row up afterwards to explain a miss.

Run a single update that sets the title and increments the version where both the id and the version match. If one row changed report ok with the next version. Otherwise read the version by id and report a conflict when a row exists and not found when none does.

fund-js/24-sql-transactions-and-app-code.instructions:
**Skills:** bound parameters · SQL injection · LIKE escaping · tenant filter  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "This product search builds its SQL by concatenation. Show me an input that breaks it, then fix it."

**Why it matters.** The query carries a tenant filter. Input that can change the shape of the statement can remove that filter, and then a search box lists other customers' data. Binding the values closes that hole, and leaves a smaller one: the wildcard characters of `LIKE`.

**The database.** `db` is a synchronous SQLite handle (Node's `node:sqlite`): `db.prepare(sql).all(...params)` returns the rows. The table is `products(id, tenant_id, name)`.

**Your task.** Export `searchProducts(db, tenantId, term)`. It returns an array of `{ id, name }` objects: the products of that tenant whose name contains `term`, ordered by name and then id.
- matching uses SQLite's `LIKE`, which ignores ASCII letter case
- no value of `term` or `tenantId` may ever return another tenant's rows or throw a syntax error
- a quote in the term is an ordinary character
- a percent sign or an underscore in the term matches only that character
- an empty term returns all of the tenant's products

**Worked example.** For tenant 1 the term `mug` finds "Travel mug" and "Blue MUG large". The term `%` finds only "50% cotton tee".
fund-js/24-sql-transactions-and-app-code.explanation:
```js
const escaped = String(term).replace(/[\\%_]/g, (ch) => '\\' + ch);
return db
  .prepare("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE tenant_id = ? AND name LIKE ? ESCAPE '\\' ORDER BY name, id")
  .all(tenantId, '%' + escaped + '%')
  .map((row) => ({ id: row.id, name: row.name }));
```

Both values are bound. The statement the database parses contains two placeholders and nothing from the user, so `' OR 1=1 --` is simply a string that no product name contains. The tenant filter is bound too: a number glued into SQL is just as injectable as a string.

The plausible wrong answer stops at "I used parameters": it binds `'%' + term + '%'` unchanged. Injection is gone, but a term of `%` or `_` is still a wildcard and returns the tenant's whole catalogue. The boundary test catches it. Escape the two wildcards and the escape character itself, and name that character with `ESCAPE`.

Doubling quotes by hand is the other tempting repair. It is easy to get wrong for one dialect or another, and it does nothing for the tenant id.

Postgres uses the same `LIKE ... ESCAPE` rules, numbered placeholders, and `ILIKE` for a case-insensitive match, since its `LIKE` is case-sensitive.
hints: Keep the statement and the data apart: the statement text must be the same for every input.
Hand both the tenant and the search pattern to the database as values, never as part of the statement text. Then deal with the two characters that still have a special meaning inside a pattern.

Put a backslash in front of every backslash, percent sign and underscore in the term, wrap the result in percent signs, and bind it together with the tenant id to a statement whose pattern comparison declares the backslash as its escape character.
